title: Stark Schoolhouse
alt: People on ladders painting the exterior of the white Stark Schoolhouse
summary: A 2020 grant helped the Ninemile Community Center buy paint for the exterior of the historic Stark Schoolhouse.
paragraphs: One of several mining towns to spring up in the Ninemile Valley after gold was discovered in 1874, Stark, founded in 1890, consisted of shops, a hotel/saloon, and the Stark, Montana Post Office which was established on June 25th of that same year. Although many of the other settlements died off when mining activities decreased, Stark managed to hang on until 1916 when the Anaconda Mining Company moved its logging operations to the Valley giving the town a second life. It continued to thrive until the ACM shut down its lumbering activities and pulled out of the valley in 1926, ending that town’s life as well.

The Stark School District of Missoula County was created in 1896 and records indicate that there was a schoolhouse built somewhere in the district at that time but the location has since been lost to history. In 1905 Frederick and Jessie Proebstel donated land to the district and in 1915 a new Stark Schoolhouse was built on the property by residents, the ACM, and the public school system, opening to students in January of 1916. Once ACM left the area, the number of residents dwindled and the school closed in 1929-30 leaving the few remaining students to be bussed to the lower Ninemile School.

The Stark School remained to serve as the center of community activities and in 1949 the building was turned over to the Ninemile community for their club house and was renamed the Ninemile Community Center, serving as such to this day. In 1995 the building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Many renovations have been performed by the Ninemile Community Center Board and the community utilizing grants, donations, and volunteer labor. In 2020, the organization applied for and received a Garnet Preservation Association License Plate Program grant and used it to buy paint for the exterior of the building, helping it to continue to be a cherished source of pride for the people of Ninemile.
One of just two buildings remaining from the historic community of Stark, Montana, the Stark schoolhouse continues to serve the residents of the Upper Ninemile area to this day.

title: Bonner Milltown History Center
alt: Two men standing beside a railroad history interpretive panel outside the Bonner Milltown History Center
summary: A 2024 grant supported Interpreting Bonner’s Railroad History, an outdoor exhibit of artifacts and interpretive signs.
paragraphs: The Garnet License Plate grant recipient in 2024 was the Bonner Milltown History Center for developing their exhibit Interpreting Bonner’s Railroad History. The History Center also partnered with Missoula County and Friends of Two Rivers to create railroad interpretive signs and install the outside exhibit. Artifacts and signage tell the story of the railroads that ran in and through the area and significantly impacted the local and surrounding communities. Located outside of the Bonner Milltown History Center, the exhibit is open to the public 24/7/365. More information about the History Center is available at https://bonnermilltownhistory.org/

title: Alberton Milwaukee Depot
summary: A 2019 grant funded replacement of three large windows in the area of the depot that houses the library.
paragraphs: The Milwaukee Railroad Depot in Alberton, constructed in the classic Craftsman style, was built by the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railway in 1908 as the “Milwaukee Road” pushed its way westward. In addition to the depot, a roundhouse with a turntable and locomotive repair shops were built on the site. The depot itself was larger than the norm and included a passenger waiting room, station master’s office, rest rooms, ticket booth, freight warehouse, and living quarters for the station master and family. It also housed a Beanery owned and operated by the railroad, where people could grab a quick bite during the 30-minute stop that the trains made on their way east and west each day.
The town of Alberton, Montana literally grew up around the depot and its facilities, employing many of the area residents in one way or another.
When the railroad was electrified in 1916, the roundhouse and turntable were removed.
The Milwaukee Railroad declared bankruptcy in 1980 and the Milwaukee line was abandoned.

The depot was sold to the Town of Alberton in 1983 and the people of Alberton, working with the Town, turned the rail yards into a city park and began to refurbish the depot utilizing grants and hard work.

In recent years a decision was made to replace the many large windows one at a time using grant funds. In the spring of 2019 the Town was awarded a Garnet Preservation Association License Plate Program grant that provided funds to replace three such windows in the area where the library is housed, moving the effort that much closer to its goal.
Listed in the National Register of Historic Places on January 13, 1997, the Alberton Milwaukee Depot still serves as the heart of the community.

title: Missoula Engine 1356
alt: Northern Pacific Engine 1356 decorated with holiday lights at night
summary: The 2025 grant supported wiring for headlights, number boards, and a cab switch, along with restoration work on the tender.
paragraphs: The 2025 recipient of the Garnet License Plate grant was The Friends of the 1356 for their project entitled Cosmetic Restoration of Historic Northern Pacific Engine 1356. Wiring for headlights, number boards, and the switch inside the cab as well as restoration work on the tender were the focus for the grant dollars. The engine is located downtown Missoula and is available for the public to enjoy day and night, all year round. Knowing that the lights on the 1356 were made possible by the License Plate Grant, it was a thrill to witness the holiday lighting of engine 1356 during the Missoula Christmas Tree Lighting event in December 2025. More information about the Friends of the 1356 is available at https://www.missoula1356.org

title: DeBorgia Schoolhouse
alt: Period-style ceiling light inside the DeBorgia Schoolhouse
summary: A 2017 grant helped purchase and install period-accurate ceiling lights, replacing fixtures used for nearly 100 years.
paragraphs: The DeBorgia Schoolhouse (No. 7, Public School), built in 1908, and located in the original town of DeBorgia, Montana, was the first two story frame building in the West End of Mineral County. When the Great Fire of 1910 came roaring through the area, the towns of DeBorgia, Saltese, and Haugan were pretty much all destroyed leaving the schoolhouse as one of the few buildings standing unscathed. The building was relocated to its present site on Thompson-De Borgia Road in 1948 where it continued to serve students in grades 1 through 8 until its closure in 1956 (some sources say 1958).

After the closure of the school, the building continued to function as a community center for the West Enders and was used for meetings, elections, performances, and social gatherings but with little regular maintenance it soon fell into disrepair. In 1969 a local group of concerned women, called the Happy Homemakers, decided to preserve it by raising funds through bake sales and other events. This group is still active to this day working to ensure that the building stays in good repair so that it can continue to be used and enjoyed by future West Enders and others who are visiting the area. Entered into the National Register of Historic Places on December 27, 1979, the schoolhouse also now serves as the local museum and is open to visitors on a limited basis.

To this day, the DeBorgia Schoolhouse continues to provide a place for events of all kinds. Members hold an annual 3-day rummage sale each June, host a county-wide apple pie sale every fall and host a spaghetti dinner the night before hunting season starts to name a few.

Along with other fundraising activities held throughout the year, small grants are sought to help with expenses. In the spring of 2017, a Garnet Preservation Association License Plate grant was awarded to the schoolhouse; members used the funds to purchase and install several period accurate ceiling lights, replacing the old lights that had been used for nearly 100 years!
